newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY GOVT. SEC YIELDS SEEN STABLE AFTER MAY C/A.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY GOVT. SEC YIELDS SEEN STABLE AFTER MAY C/A.

text.p: A good May current account
will help Hungary's government securities yields to stabilise
after recent upward corrections of 10 to 15 basis points due to
a rise in inflation in June, traders said on Monday.
"The market is becoming quiet," said Zsolt Bango of Gog
Securities. "For the next one and a half to two months stable
interest rates can be expected."
Government securities yields reversed a several-week-long
trend of slow decline one week ago when the Central Statistical
Office reported an 18.7 percent year-on-year rise in inflation
compared with a central bank forecast of 17.4 to 17.8 percent.
The National Bank of Hungary said that 0.9 percentage
points of the 1.7 percent month-on-month rise was due to one
single factor, a 150 percent rise in potato prices.
However, traders said the market was again looking at
previous analyst forecasts for relatively high inflation
figures for the summer months due to low comparative
agricultural price levels in 1996.
"The July and August inflation figures will be the key to
government securities yields," said Zsolt Bango of
Creditanstalt Securities. "I expect a stagnation (in
year-on-year inflation) above 18 percent for the next two
months."
Traders said the May current account figures, published on
Friday and reflecting a $148 million surplus for that month,
were likely to have stopped the upward correction wave which
followed the release of the June inflation figures.
"The situation has stabilised due to the very good current
account figures," Szogi said.
Traders said that inflation was likely to continue the
previous eighteen-month-long trend of decline from September or
October and that is likely to trigger a new fall in yields and
a recovery in demand for government securities.
They added that a minor outflow of foreign funds from the
Hungarian market due to concern about the region following
uncertainties surrounding the Polish zloty also contributed to
the easing in demand and the rise in yields.
However, foreign investors were likely to be reassured by
the continued strength of the forint fed by sound economic
fundamentals, traders said.
They said they expected a minor upward technical correction
in discount treasury bill yields at this week's auctions, while
government securities yields on the secondary market were
likely to move sideways.
